claim: Brain age is a widely used index for quantifying individuals' brain health as deviation from a normative brain aging trajectory.
source: Brain age is a widely used index for quantifying individuals' brain health as deviation from a normative brain aging trajectory.
evidence: This is a statement about the current use of brain age in the field, supported by the literature context provided in the manuscript.

claim: Higher-than-expected brain age is thought partially to reflect above-average rate of brain aging.
source: Higher-than-expected brain age is thought partially to reflect above-average rate of brain aging.
evidence: This represents a common assumption in the field that the authors are testing.

claim: There is no association between cross-sectional brain age and the rate of brain change measured longitudinally.
source: The results showed no association between cross-sectional brain age and the rate of brain change measured longitudinally.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by statistical analyses in multiple datasets.

claim: Brain age in adulthood is associated with birth weight.
source: Rather, brain age in adulthood was associated with the congenital factors of birth weight and polygenic scores of brain age, assumed to reflect a constant, lifelong influence on brain structure from early life.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of birth weight data in relation to brain age delta.

claim: Brain age in adulthood is associated with polygenic scores of brain age.
source: Rather, brain age in adulthood was associated with the congenital factors of birth weight and polygenic scores of brain age, assumed to reflect a constant, lifelong influence on brain structure from early life.
evidence: This finding is supported by genetic analysis and statistical modeling in the manuscript.

claim: The biological age of the brain is estimated typically by applying machine learning to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data to predict chronological age.
source: The biological age of the brain is estimated typically by applying machine learning to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data to predict chronological age.
evidence: This describes the standard methodology in the field, which is established knowledge.

claim: Brain age delta has been related to brain, mental, and cognitive health.
source: Brain age delta has been related to brain, mental, and cognitive health, and proved valuable in predicting outcomes such as mortality (Cole et al., 2018; Cole and Franke, 2017; Elliott et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Brain age delta proved valuable in predicting outcomes such as mortality.
source: Brain age delta has been related to brain, mental, and cognitive health, and proved valuable in predicting outcomes such as mortality (Cole et al., 2018; Cole and Franke, 2017; Elliott et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is assumed that brain age delta reflects past and ongoing neurobiological aging processes.
source: To different degrees, it is assumed that brain age delta reflects past and ongoing neurobiological aging processes (Cole and Franke, 2017; Elliott et al., 2019; Franke and Gaser, 2019; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a common assumption in the field, supported by citations.

claim: It is common to interpret positive brain age deltas as reflecting a steeper rate of brain aging.
source: Hence, it is common to interpret positive brain age deltas as reflecting a steeper rate of brain aging; often dubbed as accelerated aging (here both terms are used interchangeably) (Cole and Franke, 2017; Franke and Gaser, 2019; Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a common interpretation in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Individual deviations from the expected brain age could capture constant interindividual differences in brain structure that remain stable throughout the lifespan, reflecting early genetic and environmental influences.
source: Alternatively, individual deviations from the expected brain age could capture constant interindividual differences in brain structure that remain stable throughout the lifespan, reflecting early genetic and environmental influences (Deary, 2012; Elliott et al., 2019; Walhovd et al., 2016).
evidence: This alternative hypothesis is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The UK Biobank training dataset included 38,682 participants with age range 44.8–82.6 years.
source: The model was trained on 38,682 participants (age range = 44.8–82.6 years) with a single MRI from the UK Biobank (Miller et al., 2016) using gradient boosting as implemented in XGBoost (https://xgboost.readthedocs.io) and optimized using 10-fold cross-validation and a randomized hyperparameter search.
evidence: This is a direct description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The UK Biobank test dataset included 1372 participants with two MRIs each.
source: The trained model (Figure 1e) was then used to predict brain age for an independent test dataset of 1372 participants with two MRIs each (age range = 47.2–80.6 years, mean [SD] follow-up = 2.3 [0.1] years).
evidence: This is a direct description of the test dataset used in the study.

claim: The UK Biobank test dataset had a mean follow-up of 2.3 years (SD = 0.1 years).
source: The trained model (Figure 1e) was then used to predict brain age for an independent test dataset of 1372 participants with two MRIs each (age range = 47.2–80.6 years, mean [SD] follow-up = 2.3 [0.1] years).
evidence: This is a direct description of the follow-up interval in the test dataset.

claim: The brain age model achieved a correlation of r = 0.82 between chronological and brain age in the test dataset.
source: The predictions – applied to the longitudinal test set – revealed a high correlation between chronological and brain age (r = 0.82) with mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.31 years and root mean squared error (RMSE) = 4.14 years (Figure 1f), comparable to other brain age models using UK Biobank MRI data (Cole, 2020a).
evidence: This is a direct report of the model performance metrics.

claim: The brain age model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.31 years in the test dataset.
source: The predictions – applied to the longitudinal test set – revealed a high correlation between chronological and brain age (r = 0.82) with mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.31 years and root mean squared error (RMSE) = 4.14 years (Figure 1f), comparable to other brain age models using UK Biobank MRI data (Cole, 2020a).
evidence: This is a direct report of the model performance metrics.

claim: The brain age model achieved a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 4.14 years in the test dataset.
source: The predictions – applied to the longitudinal test set – revealed a high correlation between chronological and brain age (r = 0.82) with mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.31 years and root mean squared error (RMSE) = 4.14 years (Figure 1f), comparable to other brain age models using UK Biobank MRI data (Cole, 2020a).
evidence: This is a direct report of the model performance metrics.

claim: Brain age delta at baseline and follow-up were strongly correlated (r = 0.81).
source: Brain age delta at baseline and follow-up were strongly correlated (r = 0.81).
evidence: This is a direct report of the correlation between baseline and follow-up brain age delta.

claim: The Lifebrain test dataset included 3292 unique participants with age range 18.0–94.4 years.
source: To establish generalizability, we replicated our results using a different machine learning algorithm – a LASSO-based approach (Cole, 2020a) – and an independent training and test (longitudinal) dataset from the Lifebrain consortium (Walhovd et al., 2018) with up to 11.2 years of follow-up (3292 unique participants, age range = 18.0–94.4 years; technical and biological replication).
evidence: This is a direct description of the Lifebrain replication dataset.

claim: The Lifebrain dataset had up to 11.2 years of follow-up.
source: To establish generalizability, we replicated our results using a different machine learning algorithm – a LASSO-based approach (Cole, 2020a) – and an independent training and test (longitudinal) dataset from the Lifebrain consortium (Walhovd et al., 2018) with up to 11.2 years of follow-up (3292 unique participants, age range = 18.0–94.4 years; technical and biological replication).
evidence: This is a direct description of the follow-up duration in the Lifebrain dataset.

claim: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were weakly, but negatively, associated in the UK Biobank (β = –0.016 [±0.008] delta/year, t(p) = –2.0 (.04), r2 = 0.002).
source: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were weakly, but negatively, associated in the UK Biobank (β = –0.016 [±0.008] delta/year, t(p) = –2.0 (.04), r2 = 0.002, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results, also shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were unrelated using a LASSO regression approach (β = –0.003 [±0.006] delta/year, t(p) = –0.5 (.65), r2 = 0.001).
source: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were unrelated using a LASSO regression approach (β = –0.003 [±0.006] delta/year, t(p) = –0.5 (.65), r2 = 0.001, Figure 2b), and in the Lifebrain replication sample (β = –0.007 [±0.01] delta/year, t(p) = –0.6 (.53), r2 = 0.001, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication analysis results using LASSO, also shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were unrelated in the Lifebrain replication sample (β = –0.007 [±0.01] delta/year, t(p) = –0.6 (.53), r2 = 0.001).
source: Cross-sectional and brain age deltalong were unrelated using a LASSO regression approach (β = –0.003 [±0.006] delta/year, t(p) = –0.5 (.65), r2 = 0.001, Figure 2b), and in the Lifebrain replication sample (β = –0.007 [±0.01] delta/year, t(p) = –0.6 (.53), r2 = 0.001, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication analysis results in Lifebrain, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Post-hoc equivalence tests showed that positive relationships with β > 0.010 delta/year would be rejected in all three analyses.
source: Post-hoc equivalence tests showed that positive relationships with β > 0.010 delta/year would be rejected in all three analyses, thus confirming a lack of a meaningful relationship between cross-sectional and longitudinal brain age (Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the equivalence test results, also shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cross-sectional brain age delta was unrelated to a principal component of change (β = –0.009 [±0.01] year, t(p) = –0.7 (.46), r2 = 0.001).
source: Cross-sectional brain age delta was unrelated to a principal component of change (β = –0.009 [±0.01] year, t(p) = –0.7 (.46), r2 = 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for the composite measure of brain change.

claim: Brain age deltalong was associated with a principal component of change in the UK Biobank dataset (p<0.001).
source: In contrast, brain age deltalong was associated with a principal component of change in the UK Biobank dataset as well as in both replication analyses (all tests p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results showing association between longitudinal brain age delta and composite brain change.

claim: Cross-sectional brain age delta was significantly related to change in features capturing lateral ventricle expansion and white matter hypointensities (p<0.05 Bonferroni-corrected).
source: For specific features, cross-sectional brain age delta was significantly related to change – in the expected direction – of features capturing lateral ventricle expansion and white matter hypointensities (p<0.05 Bonferroni-corrected).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for specific brain features.

claim: Brain age deltalong related to change in 45 of the features pertaining to four different modalities.
source: Brain age deltalong related to change in 45 of the features pertaining to four different modalities.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of features showing significant relationships with longitudinal brain age delta.

claim: The scaling of brain age delta throughout the datasets' age range was δ = 0.14 for the UK Biobank dataset.
source: The scaling (δ) of brain age delta (δ) throughout the datasets' age range was = 0.14 and 0.09 for the UK Biobank and the Lifebrain datasets.
evidence: This is a direct report of the scaling parameter calculated from the data.

claim: The scaling of brain age delta throughout the datasets' age range was δ = 0.09 for the Lifebrain dataset.
source: The scaling (δ) of brain age delta (δ) throughout the datasets' age range was = 0.14 and 0.09 for the UK Biobank and the Lifebrain datasets.
evidence: This is a direct report of the scaling parameter calculated from the data.

claim: The increase in the spread of brain age delta when moving from youngest to oldest was δ = 0.38 years in the UK Biobank dataset.
source: This corresponds to an increase in the spread of brain age delta of |δ| = 0.38 and 0.37 years – when moving from youngest to oldest – in the UK Biobank and the Lifebrain datasets, suggesting that brain age delta only modestly reflects rate of aging effects.
evidence: This is a direct report of the calculated spread of brain age delta across the age range.

claim: The increase in the spread of brain age delta when moving from youngest to oldest was δ = 0.37 years in the Lifebrain dataset.
source: This corresponds to an increase in the spread of brain age delta of |δ| = 0.38 and 0.37 years – when moving from youngest to oldest – in the UK Biobank and the Lifebrain datasets, suggesting that brain age delta only modestly reflects rate of aging effects.
evidence: This is a direct report of the calculated spread of brain age delta across the age range.

claim: Brain age delta only modestly reflects rate of aging effects.
source: This corresponds to an increase in the spread of brain age delta of |δ| = 0.38 and 0.37 years – when moving from youngest to oldest – in the UK Biobank and the Lifebrain datasets, suggesting that brain age delta only modestly reflects rate of aging effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the scaling analysis results.

claim: Birth weight was significantly related to brain age delta (β = –0.70 [±0.30] year/kg, t(p) = −2.3 (0.02), r2 = 0.009).
source: Birth weight was significantly related to brain age delta (β = –0.70 [±0.30] year/kg, t(p) = −2.3 (0.02), r2 = 0.009, Figure 3a), but not to delta change (β = 0.02 [±0.09] year/kg, t(p) = 0.3 (0.79), Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for birth weight, also shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Birth weight was not related to delta change (β = 0.02 [±0.09] year/kg, t(p) = 0.3 (0.79)).
source: Birth weight was significantly related to brain age delta (β = –0.70 [±0.30] year/kg, t(p) = −2.3 (0.02), r2 = 0.009, Figure 3a), but not to delta change (β = 0.02 [±0.09] year/kg, t(p) = 0.3 (0.79), Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for birth weight and longitudinal change, also shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Birth weights were limited to normal variations at full term (from 2.5 to 4.5 kg; n = 770 unique individuals).
source: Birth weights were limited to normal variations at full term (from 2.5 to 4.5 kg; n = 770 unique individuals) but see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for results with varying cutoffs.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the birth weight analysis.

claim: The birth weight results were replicated using the LASSO approach (β = –0.79 [±0.29] year/kg, t(p) = −2.8 (0.006), r2 = 0.009).
source: The results were not affected by excluding individuals being part of multiple births (p=0.02) and were replicated using the LASSO approach (β = –0.79 [±0.29] year/kg, t(p) = −2.8 (0.006), r2 = 0.009, Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication analysis results using LASSO, also shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PGS-BA was positively associated with brain age delta (β = 0.54 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 9.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02).
source: PGS-BA was positively associated with brain age delta (β = 0.54 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 9.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02, Figure 4a) and negatively associated with brain age delta change (β = –0.06 [±0.03] year, t(p) = −2.4 (0.02), Figure 4c) in the independent test dataset.
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for PGS-BA, also shown in Figure 4a.

claim: PGS-BA was negatively associated with brain age delta change (β = –0.06 [±0.03] year, t(p) = −2.4 (0.02)).
source: PGS-BA was positively associated with brain age delta (β = 0.54 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 9.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02, Figure 4a) and negatively associated with brain age delta change (β = –0.06 [±0.03] year, t(p) = −2.4 (0.02), Figure 4c) in the independent test dataset.
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical analysis results for PGS-BA and longitudinal change, also shown in Figure 4c.

claim: PGS-BA was associated with brain age delta derived from the LASSO algorithm (β = 0.53 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 10.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02).
source: Likewise, PGS-BA was associated with brain age delta derived from the LASSO algorithm (β = 0.53 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 10.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02, Figure 4b) but not to brain age delta change (β = –0.001 [±.02] year, t(p) = 0.0 (1.0), Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication analysis results using LASSO, also shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PGS-BA was not associated with brain age delta change using the LASSO algorithm (β = –0.001 [±.02] year, t(p) = 0.0 (1.0)).
source: Likewise, PGS-BA was associated with brain age delta derived from the LASSO algorithm (β = 0.53 [±0.09] year, t(p) = 10.4 (<0.001), r2 = 0.02, Figure 4b) but not to brain age delta change (β = –0.001 [±.02] year, t(p) = 0.0 (1.0), Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication analysis results using LASSO, also shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Individual variation in the cross-sectional brain age metric does not capture across-subject differences in the ongoing rate of brain aging.
source: Altogether, these findings do not support the claim that individual variation in the cross-sectional brain age metric capture across-subject differences in the ongoing rate of brain aging.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: Brain age seems to reflect early-life influences on brain structure.
source: Rather, brain age seems to reflect early-life influences on brain structure, and only to a very modest degree reflects actual rate of brain change in middle and old adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the birth weight and PGS-BA analyses.

claim: Brain age only to a very modest degree reflects actual rate of brain change in middle and old adulthood.
source: Rather, brain age seems to reflect early-life influences on brain structure, and only to a very modest degree reflects actual rate of brain change in middle and old adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal analysis results.

claim: Middle-aged individuals with higher brain age already exhibited poorer cognitive function and brain health at age 3 years.
source: An exception is Elliott et al., 2019, who found that middle-aged individuals with higher brain age already exhibited poorer cognitive function and brain health at age 3 years.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study that supports the early-life account.

claim: Childhood IQ shows lifelong, stable influences on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
source: This fits a robust corpus of literature showing effects of lifelong, stable influences as indexed by childhood IQ (Karama et al., 2014), genetics (Walhovd et al., 2020), and neonatal characteristics (Walhovd et al., 2016) on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetics show lifelong, stable influences on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
source: This fits a robust corpus of literature showing effects of lifelong, stable influences as indexed by childhood IQ (Karama et al., 2014), genetics (Walhovd et al., 2020), and neonatal characteristics (Walhovd et al., 2016) on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neonatal characteristics show lifelong, stable influences on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
source: This fits a robust corpus of literature showing effects of lifelong, stable influences as indexed by childhood IQ (Karama et al., 2014), genetics (Walhovd et al., 2020), and neonatal characteristics (Walhovd et al., 2016) on brain and cognitive variation in old age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At a population level brain age captures modest rate of aging effects because brain age delta spreads with increasing age.
source: It has been argued that at a population level brain age captures modest rate of aging effects because brain age delta spreads with increasing age (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an argument from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Brain age related to change in a few specific neuroimaging features, that is, ventricular expansion and white matter hypointensities.
source: Likewise, our secondary analyses suggested brain age related to change in a few specific neuroimaging features, that is, ventricular expansion and white matter hypointensities, though not to any composite score.
evidence: This is a finding from the secondary analyses reported in the manuscript.

claim: The largest part of interindividual variation in brain age delta originates before the sample lower bound (⪝ 18 and 45 years for the Lifebrain and UK Biobank datasets).
source: The largest part of interindividual variation in brain age delta, instead, largely originates before the sample lower bound (⪝ 18 and 45 years for the Lifebrain and UK Biobank datasets).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results showing early-life influences.

claim: Associations of brain age with other bodily markers of aging or with cognitive decline have yielded mixed support for cross-sectional brain age as a marker of individual differences in brain aging.
source: Also, associations of brain age with other bodily markers of aging or with cognitive decline have yielded mixed support for cross-sectional brain age as a marker of individual differences in brain aging (Cole et al., 2018, p. 201; Elliott et al., 2019; Franke and Gaser, 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Using independent component analysis, distinct modes of multimodal brain variation better reflect both the genetic make-up and ongoing aging effects compared to a single brain age score.
source: Using independent component analysis, a recent study found that – compared to a single brain age score – distinct modes of multimodal brain variation better reflect both the genetic make-up and ongoing aging effects, with a subset of modes showing significant spreading of delta with age (Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Without longitudinal imaging, one should not interpret brain age as accelerated aging.
source: Yet, without longitudinal imaging, one should not interpret brain age as accelerated aging.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Covariance structures capturing differences between individuals do not necessarily generalize to covariance structures within individuals.
source: Our results align with theoretical claims and empirical observations that covariance structures capturing differences between individuals do not necessarily generalize to covariance structures within individuals (Molenaar, 2004; Schmiedek et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle supported by citations.

claim: Cross-sectional brain age has low validity as an index of brain aging despite having high reliability.
source: From a measurement theory perspective, our results suggest that cross-sectional brain age has low validity as an index of brain aging – despite having high reliability (Franke and Gaser, 2012) – as only a small portion of variance is associated with the trait of interest alone (Zuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from a measurement theory perspective, supported by citations.

claim: Birth weight reflects differences in genetic propensities and prenatal environment.
source: The results further showed that birth weight, which reflects differences in genetic propensities and prenatal environment (Gielen et al., 2008), explained a modest portion of the variance in brain age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Subtle variations in birth weight are associated with brain structure early in life and present throughout the lifespan.
source: Subtle variations in birth weight are associated with brain structure early in life and present throughout the lifespan (Walhovd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Brain development is strongly influenced by a genetic architecture that, in interaction with environmental factors, leads to substantial, longlasting effects on brain structure.
source: These findings link with evidence that brain development is strongly influenced by a genetic architecture that, in interaction with environmental factors, leads to substantial, longlasting effects on brain structure.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain development supported by the study findings and broader literature.

claim: Aging mechanisms seem to be more related to limitations of maintenance and repair functions and have a more stochastic nature.
source: By contrast, aging mechanisms seem to be more related to limitations of maintenance and repair functions and have a more stochastic nature (Kirkwood, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Self-reported birth weight is a highly reliable measure.
source: Self-reported birth weight (Nilsen et al., 2017) and cross-sectional brain age (Franke and Gaser, 2012) are highly reliable measures; thus, our analyses are well-powered to detect small effects (Zuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cross-sectional brain age is a highly reliable measure.
source: Self-reported birth weight (Nilsen et al., 2017) and cross-sectional brain age (Franke and Gaser, 2012) are highly reliable measures; thus, our analyses are well-powered to detect small effects (Zuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Brain age delta is a prediction error from a model that maximizes the prediction of age in cross-sectional data and thus partially also reflects noise.
source: Strictly speaking, brain age delta is a prediction error from a model that maximizes the prediction of age in cross-sectional data and thus partially also reflects noise.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the nature of brain age delta.

claim: Changes in brain age are partly heritable.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have found that changes in brain age are partly heritable (Brouwer et al., 2021) and relate to, for instance, cardiometabolic risk factors (Beck, 2021), suggesting that it captures biologically relevant signals (i.e., has predictive validity), although with substantially different origins from cross-sectional brain age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Changes in brain age relate to cardiometabolic risk factors.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have found that changes in brain age are partly heritable (Brouwer et al., 2021) and relate to, for instance, cardiometabolic risk factors (Beck, 2021), suggesting that it captures biologically relevant signals (i.e., has predictive validity), although with substantially different origins from cross-sectional brain age.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Birth weight and genetic risk for neurodegenerative conditions affect brain structure from early life.
source: There is considerable evidence in the literature that birth weight and genetic risk for neurodegenerative conditions affect brain structure from early life (Raznahan et al., 2012; Walhovd et al., 2020; Walhovd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Brain age models are related to other models such as normative brain charts.
source: Brain age models are related to other models such as normative brain charts (Bethlehem, 2021; Dong et al., 2020) – akin to normative anthropometric charts – the main difference being that brain age models predict, rather than control for, age (Marquand et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological approaches, supported by citations.

claim: The main difference between brain age models and normative brain charts is that brain age models predict, rather than control for, age.
source: Brain age models are related to other models such as normative brain charts (Bethlehem, 2021; Dong et al., 2020) – akin to normative anthropometric charts – the main difference being that brain age models predict, rather than control for, age (Marquand et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological distinction, supported by a citation.

claim: Both brain age models and normative brain charts produce normative brain scores, which are uncorrelated with age.
source: Both types of models produce normative brain scores, which are uncorrelated with age (Butler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characteristic of these models, supported by a citation.

claim: Caution is required when interpreting normative brain scores as indices of brain aging without availability of longitudinal data.
source: Thus, caution is required when interpreting these scores as indices of brain aging without availability of longitudinal data.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Developmental samples may reflect slightly stronger relationships between cross-sectional brain age delta and ongoing brain change as brain changes during early-life development typically occur at a faster pace than in middle or later life.
source: Developmental samples may, however, reflect slightly stronger relationships between cross-sectional brain age delta and ongoing brain change as brain changes during early-life development typically occur at a faster pace than in middle or later life.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the findings might differ in developmental samples.

claim: For specific disease groups such as Alzheimer's disease patients, interindividual brain variation in brain age might reflect to a greater extent prevailing loss of brain structure.
source: Similarly, for specific disease groups such as Alzheimer's disease patients (Franke and Gaser, 2012), interindividual brain variation in brain age might reflect to a greater extent prevailing loss of brain structure.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the findings might differ in disease populations, with a citation.

claim: As time from birth increases, chronological age as a marker of individual development is reduced.
source: That is, as time from birth increases, chronological age as a marker of individual development is reduced.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between age and developmental markers.

claim: Birth weight and PGS-BA are paradigmatic for showing how interindividual differences in brain age emerge early in life.
source: Thus, birth weight and PGS-BA are paradigmatic for showing how interindividual differences in brain age emerge early in life.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses of birth weight and PGS-BA.

claim: The results call for caution in interpreting brain-derived indices of aging based on cross-sectional MRI data.
source: The results call for caution in interpreting brain-derived indices of aging based on cross-sectional MRI data and underscore the need to rely on longitudinal data whenever the goal is to understand the trajectories of brain and cognition in aging.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: There is a need to rely on longitudinal data whenever the goal is to understand the trajectories of brain and cognition in aging.
source: The results call for caution in interpreting brain-derived indices of aging based on cross-sectional MRI data and underscore the need to rely on longitudinal data whenever the goal is to understand the trajectories of brain and cognition in aging.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Chronological age was predicted based on 365 regional and global features from structural T1w MRI.
source: Chronological age (Figure 1c) was predicted based on regional and global features from structural T1w MRI, including cortical thickness, area, volume, and gray-white matter contrast, as well as subcortical volume and intensity imaging-derived phenotypes (|N| = 365).
evidence: This describes the features used in the brain age model.

claim: The brain age model was trained using gradient boosting as implemented in XGBoost.
source: The model was trained on 38,682 participants (age range = 44.8–82.6 years) with a single MRI from the UK Biobank (Miller et al., 2016) using gradient boosting as implemented in XGBoost (https://xgboost.readthedocs.io) and optimized using 10-fold cross-validation and a randomized hyperparameter search.
evidence: This describes the machine learning method used.

claim: The brain age model was optimized using 10-fold cross-validation and a randomized hyperparameter search.
